notes.meaning: Solomon built a massive bronze altar for animal sacrifices. It measured about thirty feet long and wide, and fifteen feet high, making it much larger than the altar Moses made for the tabernacle. Because Israel had grown so much, a larger altar was needed to handle many more offerings. Its height also let the worshipping crowd see the fire and be reminded of God's holiness and mercy.

Solomon made a gigantic round basin out of cast bronze, called the Sea because of the huge amount of water it held. It was about fifteen feet across from rim to rim, seven and a half feet deep, and forty-five feet around. It replaced the smaller washing basin used in the wilderness tent, providing plenty of water for temple ceremonies.

Small figures shaped like oxen were cast directly into the bronze below the basin's rim, running around it in two rows. Ten carved figures were placed in every cubit of distance around the circle. These decorations were cast in the same mold as the basin itself rather than welded on later.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars note that the parallel text in 1 Kings describes wild gourds rather than oxen around the rim, which could be an early copyist error since the two Hebrew words look very similar, though others suggest both designs may have been included.

notes.meaning: The great basin sat upon twelve full-sized bronze oxen arranged in four groups of three. Each group faced outward toward one of the four main directions of the compass—north, west, south, and east—with their hindquarters turned inward toward the center. This design provided a solid base and pictured strength extending in every direction.

The bronze walls of the Sea were about three inches thick, and the upper rim flared outward like a cup shaped like an open lily flower. It could hold about three thousand baths, which equals thousands of gallons of water. This vast supply showed how completely God provides for spiritual cleansing.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Commentators often harmonize the three thousand baths mentioned here with the two thousand baths in 1 Kings by explaining that three thousand was the total capacity when full to the brim, while two thousand was the amount normally kept inside for daily use.

notes.meaning: Solomon also made ten smaller bronze basins, placing five on the south side of the courtyard and five on the north side. The priests used these smaller basins to rinse the pieces of meat for the burnt offerings. The huge Sea was kept separate and used only for the priests to wash their hands and feet before serving.

Ten lampstands made of solid gold were placed inside the holy room of the temple, five on the south wall and five on the north wall. They were crafted according to the original instructions God had given to Moses for the tabernacle. Multiplying the lampstands from one to ten brought much brighter light into the enlarged house of God.

Solomon placed ten tables inside the temple, five on the north side and five on the south side, along with one hundred gold bowls. These tables held the sacred bread that was regularly presented before God. The bowls were used by the priests to handle offerings and pour out sacred liquids during worship.

Solomon laid out two courtyards: an inner court reserved for the priests and a large outer court where the rest of the people could gather. The wooden doors leading into the courts were covered in sheets of bronze. This bronze plating protected the wood from bad weather and added strength and dignity to the entrance.

The great bronze Sea was placed on the south side of the courtyard, toward the southeast corner. This position put it right between the bronze altar and the entrance of the temple building. It gave the priests easy access to clean water before they entered the holy place.

Huram, the skilled metal craftsman, made the ash pots, shovels, and small bowls used at the bronze altar. With these items, he successfully completed all the metalwork he had agreed to create for King Solomon's temple.

The inventory begins with the two large bronze pillars that stood at the temple porch, along with their bowl-shaped tops. Huram also fashioned bronze latticework that wrapped around each capital like a protective net.

Huram crafted four hundred bronze pomegranates to hang on the latticework of the two pillars. They were arranged in two rows around each top section to give the entrance a rich and beautiful appearance.

Next, the list records the ten movable bronze stands and the washing basins that rested upon them. These wheeled carts let the temple workers roll water wherever it was needed for cleaning sacrifices.
The list also includes the giant Sea and the twelve bronze oxen that carried it on their backs. These large pieces were among the most striking metal structures in the entire courtyard.

Huram-abi crafted the pots for ashes, the shovels, the meat hooks, and all related tools out of polished bronze. The title given to him shows he was honored as a master artist and trusted adviser to the king.

King Solomon had all these bronze objects cast in the Jordan River valley between the towns of Succoth and Zeredah. The soil there had dense, clay-rich earth that worked well for shaping large casting molds. Melting and pouring the metal in this valley kept the heavy foundry work away from the temple site itself.

Solomon ordered these bronze furnishings in such vast quantities that no one ever weighed the metal used. The king gave without keeping a strict score of his expenses, gladly dedicating all the bronze to God's service.

Solomon turned from bronze to gold for the furnishings inside the temple building. He made the golden altar used for burning fragrant incense, as well as the tables that held the Bread of the Presence. This special bread was set out before God weekly as a reminder of His ongoing care and fellowship with the twelve tribes.

The lampstands and their lamps were made of pure gold to burn in front of the Most Holy Place, exactly as God's law directed. Their continual light reminded the priests that God is the true source of guidance and life for His people.
The flower-shaped decorations, the oil lamps, and the tongs used to care for the wicks were fashioned out of solid, top-quality gold. Nothing cheap or impure was permitted near God's dwelling place.

All the smaller tools—wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, spoons, and incense firepans—were made of pure gold, and the temple doors were covered with gold plating. This included both the inner doors leading into the Most Holy Place and the doors to the main hall. Every part of the building, down to the smallest tool, was treated with holy reverence.
